en.title: International Relations: the whole course
en.short: What International Relations is, how the degree is organised, the main areas, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: International Relations (IR) is the study of how states, international organisations, firms, non-governmental organisations and people interact across borders. It asks who gets what, when and how in world politics, and why order is possible without a world government. Core ideas include sovereignty (supreme authority within a state’s borders), anarchy, power, legitimacy and order. IR is a social science: it builds theories, compares cases and uses evidence, but it also draws on history, law, economics and philosophy. It is not the same as international law or diplomacy, though it studies both. It is also not simply the news. A good IR student can explain an event with a theory, name the assumptions, and say what evidence would support or weaken the explanation. Where scholars disagree, the course sets out each view and its reasoning.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text: Degree structures differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, International Relations is commonly studied as a BSc or BA in a department of political science or international relations, and programmes follow National Universities Commission benchmarks. A bachelor’s degree commonly takes four years in Nigeria, though some institutions differ. In the United Kingdom, a bachelor’s usually takes three years; in the United States, four. Polytechnics and colleges may offer related diplomas. A master’s usually takes one to two years and ends with a dissertation; lengths and awards vary. The first year builds foundations in politics, history, economics and study skills. Later years add theory, methods and specialised issues. The final year often includes a project. A master’s deepens theory and research methods and requires independent work.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually starts with the discipline itself: what IR is, its core concepts of sovereignty, anarchy, power and order, the historical evolution of the international system, actors and levels of analysis, polarity and the balance of power, international law and organisations, international political economy, security, war and peace, and methods and evidence. These introductory topics give you the vocabulary and the map.

The core then turns to theory: realism and neorealism; liberalism and neoliberal institutionalism; constructivism, identity and norms; and critical, feminist and postcolonial approaches. Theory is applied through foreign policy analysis, diplomacy and negotiation, international security and strategy, conflict resolution and peacebuilding, international organisations and global governance, international law and human rights, global trade, finance and multinational corporations, development and global inequality, regional integration and African institutions, environment, climate change and global governance, and transnational security threats. A research design and data course usually runs alongside these.

At master’s level, advanced IR theory and advanced research methods come first, and the dissertation usually comes at the end. Students then often specialise in fields such as critical security studies or global political economy, or in regional or thematic fields.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study IR by combining theory, history and evidence. For each theory, learn its core assumptions, its view of the state, its explanation of cooperation and conflict, and its main criticisms. Apply it to two cases, one from Africa and one from another region, and note what it explains well and what it misses.

Read primary documents where possible: treaties, UN resolutions, court judgments, national statements and official statistics. Use news for events, not as your only source. Keep a timeline and a map. In essays, define terms, state your question, compare explanations, and cite evidence. Learn to write short policy briefs as well as long essays. For methods, practise linking a research question to a design, a case selection and a source of data.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
The commonest mistake is to treat IR as current affairs and describe events without a question or theory. Another is to use anarchy to mean chaos; in IR it means the absence of a central world government, not the absence of order. Students also confuse the state with the government, or the nation with the state.

Many essays assert that one theory is simply true. Name the assumptions and the evidence. Do not confuse what is legal with what is just, or what is moral with what is lawful. Do not use correlation as proof of causation. Avoid generalising from one country to the world. Cite every factual claim and check the date and definition of statistics. Finally, do not ignore African agency: African states, institutions and people shape world politics, not only receive it.

keyPoints: International Relations studies how states and other actors interact across borders, and why order is possible without world government.
Sovereignty and anarchy are starting concepts, not slogans; anarchy means no central world authority, not chaos.
Theories are lenses: learn each one’s assumptions, explanations and criticisms, and apply it to cases.
Degree length and awards vary by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Use primary documents and reliable data, and distinguish correlation from causation.
African states and institutions shape world politics, not only respond to it.

en.title: International Relations as a Discipline
en.short: What IR studies, its roots in diplomatic history and law, its links to other disciplines, subfields and practice.

sections.heading: What the field covers
sections.text: International Relations (IR) is the systematic study of interactions across state borders. It asks how states, international organisations, firms, non-governmental organisations and individuals cooperate, compete and influence one another. Topics include war and peace, trade and finance, law, diplomacy, development, environment and human rights. IR is not only about states, though states remain central. It studies patterns and tries to explain them, not just describe events.

sections.heading: How it grew
sections.text: IR grew from two older bodies of work. Diplomatic history examined treaties, foreign ministries and the records of statesmen. International law studied rules that states accepted among themselves. Early scholars combined these to ask why wars occur and how law and institutions might limit them. The discipline is often dated to the period after the First World War, when governments and universities sought to understand the causes of war. It later borrowed theories and methods from political science.

sections.heading: Neighbouring disciplines
sections.text: Political science supplies concepts such as power, institutions and legitimacy, but IR applies them to relations outside a single state. Economics explains trade, finance and incentives; this overlap is international political economy. History provides evidence about change and continuity, and warns against assuming the present is unique. IR also uses sociology, law and philosophy. A good analyst uses these neighbours without treating any one as sufficient.

sections.heading: Subfields and practice
sections.text:
Main subfields include international security, international political economy, international law and organisations, foreign policy analysis, regional studies, and IR theory and methods. These overlap. For example, a study of a trade dispute may use economics, law and foreign policy analysis.

IR as a field is not the same as international politics as a practice. Practice is what governments, diplomats, firms and activists actually do. Suppose Nigeria and Ghana disagree over a border trade rule. Officials negotiate; that is practice. A scholar asks why similar disputes escalate in some cases and settle in others; that is IR. The two inform each other, but the scholar aims at general explanation, while the practitioner aims at a decision.

keyPoints: International Relations is the systematic study of interactions across state borders, not only relations between governments.
IR grew from diplomatic history and international law and became a distinct field especially after the First World War.
Political science, economics and history are close neighbours, and IR borrows concepts and evidence from them.
Main subfields include security, international political economy, international law and organisations, foreign policy analysis and theory.
IR as a field of study seeks general explanations; international politics as a practice is what actors actually do.
States remain central in IR, but the field also studies international organisations, firms, NGOs and individuals.

en.title: Core Concepts: Sovereignty, Anarchy, Power and Order
en.short: Defines state, sovereignty, anarchy, power, legitimacy, security, interdependence and globalisation.

sections.heading: State and sovereignty
sections.text:
A state has a defined territory, a permanent population, a government and the capacity to enter relations with other states. This checklist comes from the Montevideo Convention of 1933, a treaty of the Americas that textbooks still use.

Sovereignty is supreme authority: the state claims the last word inside its territory (internal), and independence outside it (external). Both claims are contested, because human rights law, aid conditions and intervention limit what governments actually do.

sections.heading: Anarchy and order
sections.text: Anarchy means the absence of a central authority above states, not chaos. Order is the pattern of rules and settled expectations that makes cooperation possible. Realists ground order in power and the balance of power, liberals in institutions and trade, and the English School in a shared society of states. They disagree about what anarchy permits.

sections.heading: Power and legitimacy
sections.text: Power is the ability to make others do, or accept, what they otherwise would not. Steven Lukes (1974) named three faces: open decisions, setting the agenda, and shaping what people think they want. Legitimacy is the belief that a rule or ruler is right; Max Weber traced it to tradition, charisma and legal-rational rules. Accepted power is cheaper than enforced power.

sections.heading: Security, interdependence, globalisation
sections.text:
Security means protection from serious threats, though whether that includes poverty and disease as well as armies is disputed. Interdependence is mutual dependence; Keohane and Nye (1977) separate sensitivity, how fast effects spread, from vulnerability, how costly adjustment is. Globalisation is the intensifying flow of goods, money, people and ideas across borders.

Two neighbours, say Nigeria and Niger, share a river and a border market. Neither can dam the river or close the market without hurting itself. That shared cost is interdependence, and it pushes both to negotiate.

keyPoints: A state needs territory, population, government and capacity to deal with other states.
Sovereignty is the state’s claim to final authority at home and independence abroad, and it is limited in practice.
Anarchy means no authority above states, not disorder; order comes from power, institutions or shared rules.
Power works through decisions, agendas and beliefs, and legitimacy makes it cheaper to use.
Interdependence means mutual dependence, measured by sensitivity and vulnerability.
Globalisation intensifies cross-border flows but does not abolish the state; its effects are disputed.

en.title: The Historical Evolution of the International System
en.short: Westphalia, Vienna, world wars, Cold War, decolonisation and debates about periodisation.

sections.heading: Westphalia to Vienna
sections.text:
The conventional account treats the Peace of Westphalia (1648) as the birth of the modern state system. It ended the Thirty Years’ War and recognised territorial rulers’ authority in religion and government. Sovereignty here means a state’s supreme authority within its territory.

After Napoleon’s defeat, the Congress of Vienna (1814-1815) redrew Europe. It sought a balance of power among great powers, the strongest states, and created the Concert of Europe, a habit of consultation among them.

sections.heading: Wars and the Cold War
sections.text:
The First World War (1914-1918) ended with the Treaty of Versailles (1919), the League of Nations and the mandate system, under which victors governed former German and Ottoman colonies for the League. The Second World War (1939-1945) produced the United Nations in 1945 and the Bretton Woods institutions from 1944 talks.

The Cold War was a bipolar rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, with alliances, nuclear deterrence and proxy wars. It ended with the Soviet collapse in 1991. The post-Cold War period saw new states from the Soviet and Yugoslav break-ups and deeper globalisation.

sections.heading: Decolonisation and expansion
sections.text:
After 1945, decolonisation, the ending of European colonial rule, brought many new states into the system. Ghana’s independence in 1957 is one example; it joined the United Nations that year. The state system expanded from Europe into Asia, Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.

Many new borders came from colonial maps, and some cut through communities. This helped create later territorial disputes. The expansion changed international politics: newly independent states used the UN to press for sovereignty, development and racial equality.

sections.heading: Qualifying the account
sections.text: Historians qualify the Westphalian story. Sovereignty emerged gradually, and imperial and religious authorities persisted. The Holy Roman Empire survived until 1806. Non-European regions had their own diplomatic orders. Periodisation, the dividing of history into eras, also varies: some start in the 1500s, others at 1648, 1815, 1919, 1945 or 1989.

keyPoints: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) is conventionally seen as the start of the modern sovereign state system.
The Congress of Vienna (1814-1815) tried to restore order through a balance of power and great-power consultation.
The two world wars produced the League of Nations, the UN and the Bretton Woods institutions.
The Cold War was a bipolar US-Soviet rivalry that ended with the Soviet collapse in 1991.
Decolonisation after 1945 expanded the state system, especially in Africa and Asia.
Historians qualify the Westphalian story and disagree about how to periodise the system.

en.title: Actors and Levels of Analysis
en.short: States, international bodies, firms, armed groups and individuals, and the three levels of analysis.

sections.heading: Actors in world politics
sections.text: An actor is any entity whose actions affect international outcomes. States are usually treated as the main actors: each has territory, population, government and capacity to act abroad. International organisations include intergovernmental organisations (IGOs), whose members are states, such as the African Union. Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) are private bodies such as Amnesty International. Multinational corporations (MNCs) own or control production in more than one country. Armed groups, from rebels to militias, use force and may hold territory. Individuals act as leaders, officials, voters, activists and victims.

sections.heading: Three levels of analysis
sections.text: Levels of analysis decide where to look for causes. The individual level focuses on people: leaders’ beliefs, personalities and choices. The state level focuses on domestic structures: regime type, institutions, bureaucracies, interest groups and public opinion. The international-system level focuses on the shared setting: distribution of power, alliances, international law, norms and global markets. The levels interact. A decision may be shaped by a leader, domestic pressure and systemic constraints at once.

sections.heading: Case: The Gambia
sections.text: In December 2016 Yahya Jammeh, president of The Gambia, rejected his election defeat. The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) mediated and threatened force; Jammeh left office in January 2017. An individual-level account stresses Jammeh’s refusal and mediators’ calculations. A state-level account stresses Gambian institutions, the army’s stance and neighbours’ interests. A system-level account stresses regional norms against unconstitutional change and ECOWAS’s role.

sections.heading: Why the level matters
sections.text: Choosing a level shapes explanation, evidence and policy advice. An individual-level account of a war may recommend changing leaders or negotiating with them. A state-level account may recommend institutional reform or power sharing. A system-level account may recommend balancing, sanctions or stronger international rules. Good analysis states its level openly and asks whether another level gives a better account. No level is always best.

keyPoints: An actor is any entity whose actions affect international outcomes.
States, IGOs, NGOs, multinational corporations, armed groups and individuals are all actors, with different resources and legitimacy.
The individual level explains through leaders’ beliefs and choices.
The state level explains through domestic institutions, regime type and interest groups.
The international-system level explains through power distribution, alliances, law and norms.
Choosing a level shapes the causes, evidence and remedies an analysis highlights.

en.title: Power, Polarity and the Balance of Power
en.short: Power in IR, polarity types, balance of power, and their limits.

sections.heading: Understanding power
sections.text: In IR, power is the ability to influence others. It has material parts: military forces, economic output, population, territory, resources and technology. It also has relational parts: power depends on the issue, opponent and setting. Nye’s soft power is attraction through culture, values and policies rather than coercion. Analysts use GDP, military spending or composite capability indices, but each measure is partial. A large economy may not become military strength, and material strength may not produce influence.

sections.heading: Polarity
sections.text: Polarity describes how capabilities are distributed among the most powerful states. Unipolarity means one state is clearly preponderant, as the United States was after the Cold War. Bipolarity means two great powers dominate, as in the Cold War between the United States and the Soviet Union. Multipolarity means several great powers share top rank, as in nineteenth-century Europe. Polarity is structural. The number of poles is disputed, because power is hard to rank and states may be strong in one area and weak in another.

sections.heading: Balance of power
sections.text: The balance of power is both a pattern and a policy. As a pattern, it is a rough equilibrium in which no state or alliance can dominate. As a policy, states balance against a threatening power. Internal balancing means building arms and capacity. External balancing means forming alliances. Stephen Walt argues that states balance against threats, not only raw power. Suppose a West African state, Aduma, expands its navy. Neighbours may seek allies or joint exercises rather than wait. Balancing can fail: states may bandwagon with the strong, pass the burden, or misread intentions.

sections.heading: Limits and debate
sections.text: These concepts are useful but contested. Power is multidimensional, so one measure hides differences. Polarity is often identified after the event and can miss middle powers and non-state actors. Balance-of-power theory predicts resistance to hegemony, but history shows balancing and bandwagoning. Critics call it vague; defenders say it captures a recurring logic of anarchy.

keyPoints: Power is the ability to influence outcomes and has material and relational dimensions.
Polarity is the number of great powers in the system: unipolar, bipolar or multipolar.
The balance of power is both an equilibrium pattern and a policy of countering a threatening state.
Internal balancing uses arms; external balancing uses alliances.
Balancing can fail through bandwagoning, buck-passing or misperception.
Power and polarity are hard to measure, so the concepts remain debated.

en.title: International Law and Organisations: An Introduction
en.short: Treaties, custom, state consent, the UN and other bodies, and why international law is hard to enforce.

sections.heading: Sources of law
sections.text: International law is the body of rules that states and other international actors treat as binding. Article 38(1) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice lists its sources. Treaties are written agreements, usually between states, governed by international law. Custom is general state practice accepted as law: practice must be widespread and consistent, and states must believe it is legally required (opinio juris). General principles fill gaps. Judicial decisions and scholarly writings are subsidiary means, not independent sources.

sections.heading: Consent and obligation
sections.text: State consent is central. A state is bound by a treaty it ratifies and by customary rules whether or not it has expressly accepted them. Consent explains why international law is not a world government. But consent is not absolute: a new state is generally bound by existing custom, and a persistent objector can escape a new custom while it objects. Peremptory norms, such as the bans on genocide and slavery, bind all states whatever their consent. These limits are debated.

sections.heading: UN and other bodies
sections.text: The United Nations is a treaty-based organisation of states. The General Assembly debates and recommends; its resolutions are usually non-binding. The Security Council can adopt binding decisions under Article 25 of the UN Charter. The International Court of Justice hears disputes between states that consent to its jurisdiction. Specialised agencies, the World Trade Organization and the International Criminal Court have legal powers. Regional bodies make and apply law.

sections.heading: Law and politics
sections.text: Law and politics overlap. Law gives reasons and procedures; politics decides interests and power. A government may obey a rule because it is legal, or because it fears sanctions. Enforcement is difficult because there is no world police. Compliance depends on reciprocity, domestic courts and Security Council action. In Nicaragua v United States (1986), the ICJ found the United States had breached customary law by supporting the contras, rebels fighting Nicaragua’s government, and mining Nicaraguan harbours. The United States rejected the judgment, and a Security Council resolution could not pass because of its veto. Law can shape debate and cost reputation.

keyPoints: The main sources of international law are treaties, custom and general principles, with judicial decisions and writings as subsidiary means.
Custom requires widespread and consistent state practice plus a belief that the practice is legally required (opinio juris).
State consent is central, but peremptory norms bind all states and a persistent objector can resist a new custom.
General Assembly resolutions are usually non-binding, while Security Council decisions under Article 25 of the UN Charter can bind states.
The ICJ decides disputes between states only when they consent to its jurisdiction.
Enforcement is difficult because there is no world police; compliance depends on reciprocity, reputation, domestic courts and Security Council action.

en.title: International Political Economy: An Introduction
en.short: How states and markets interact across borders through trade, finance, investment and development.

sections.heading: What IPE studies
sections.text: International political economy (IPE) studies how states and markets interact across borders. States make rules, tax, spend and regulate. Markets coordinate buyers, sellers, lenders and investors through prices. IPE asks how these two organise trade in goods and services, finance (cross-border loans and currency flows), investment (such as a foreign firm building a factory) and development (lasting rises in income and wellbeing). It treats them as one subject because each crosses the border between politics and economics.

sections.heading: Main questions
sections.text: The field’s main questions are: who gains and who loses from openness? Does trade or capital movement constrain government policy? Why do some countries grow and others stay poor? And who writes the rules? Economic explanations begin from scarcity, prices, incentives and efficiency. They ask which arrangement produces more output. Political explanations begin from power, interests, institutions and conflict. They ask whose support a policy needs and who bears its costs. The two often disagree because they answer different questions, not because one is simply wrong.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Imagine Aminu’s garment workshop in Kano, Nigeria, buys imported cloth. The government raises a tariff, a tax on imports. An economic account measures the extra price paid by tailors and consumers, the gain to domestic cloth makers and the tariff revenue. A political account asks which producers lobbied, which officials backed the rule, and whether the government needed support from a textile region. Both accounts can be correct.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: IPE matters because the same rule can raise national income and still be resisted. A loan, a tariff or an investment rule creates winners and losers, and losers often organise politically. Students should therefore ask two questions together: is the policy efficient, and is it politically sustainable? The answers can differ, and that gap is the subject.

keyPoints: IPE studies how states and markets interact across borders in trade, finance, investment and development.
Economic explanations stress scarcity, prices, incentives and efficiency.
Political explanations stress power, interests, institutions and distributional conflict.
The same policy can be efficient in aggregate and still create losers who resist it.
Trade, finance, investment and development are linked, so a rule in one area affects the others.
Ask both who gains and who decides, because efficiency and political sustainability are different tests.

en.title: Security, War and Peace: An Introduction
en.short: State and human security, causes of war, peace, and institutions that limit conflict.

sections.heading: Meanings of security
sections.text:
Security has no single meaning. Traditionally it means protecting a state’s territory, people and sovereignty from military attack. This is national or military security, with the state as main provider and war as main threat.

Human security shifts focus to individuals. It asks whether people are free from fear and free from want. The United Nations Development Programme popularised the idea in its 1994 Human Development Report, listing economic, food, health, environmental, personal, community and political dimensions. Critics call it broad and hard to measure; supporters say it catches threats such as famine and displacement that military security misses.

sections.heading: Causes of war
sections.text:
Wars have many causes. Common causes include disputes over territory, security fears that drive arms races, nationalism, weak states, economic rivalry and misperception by leaders. A security dilemma arises when one state’s defensive steps look threatening, so each arms in turn.

No single cause explains every war. The civil war in Sierra Leone, which ran from 1991 to 2002, for example, was shaped by weak state institutions, diamond control and regional involvement. Local and international factors combined.

sections.heading: Peace and restraint
sections.text:
Peace is more than a ceasefire. Negative peace is the absence of direct war. Positive peace adds the absence of structural violence and some measure of justice, so it addresses poverty, exclusion and repression that can feed conflict.

Institutions and strategies try to prevent or limit war. The United Nations Charter generally prohibits the threat or use of force, except in self-defence or with Security Council authorisation under Chapter VII. The Security Council can impose sanctions or authorise peacekeeping. Peacekeeping, though not named in the Charter, developed in practice. Other tools include mediation, arms control and disarmament, deterrence and alliances. Each has limits: the veto can block the Council, sanctions can harm civilians, and deterrence can fuel arms races. In 1990, ECOWAS sent ECOMOG to Liberia during its civil war, showing regional organisations can act when wider bodies are slow.

keyPoints: Security can mean state military defence or human freedom from fear and want.
Common causes of war include territorial disputes, security fears, nationalism, weak states, economic rivalry and misperception.
Negative peace is the absence of war; positive peace also addresses structural violence and injustice.
The UN Charter generally prohibits force except in self-defence or with Security Council authorisation under Chapter VII.
Peacekeeping, mediation, arms control, deterrence and alliances can limit conflict but each has limits.
Regional bodies such as ECOWAS can intervene, as ECOMOG did in Liberia in 1990.

en.title: Methods and Evidence in International Relations
en.short: How IR scholars define concepts, choose cases, gather evidence and test causal claims, with research ethics.

sections.heading: Concepts and variables
sections.text: Research begins with concepts, which are ideas such as power or mediation. A variable is a concept that can take different values, such as the number of mediation attempts. Operationalisation means saying exactly how a concept will be measured. Amina asks whether international election observers reduce election violence. She defines an observer mission as a team invited by the government and accredited. Election violence is measured as reported deaths in the election month. Observer presence is the independent variable, the proposed cause. Violence is the dependent variable, the proposed effect.

sections.heading: Cases and comparison
sections.text: A case is one unit of study, such as a country, an election or a treaty. A case study examines one case in depth. Comparison examines two or more cases chosen to test an argument. Amina compares two similar districts, one with observers and one without. If the districts differ in income or policing, those differences are confounding variables. They can make the comparison misleading. Choosing cases only where observers went is selection bias. Good comparison tries to hold other things equal or to account for them.

sections.heading: Documents and interviews
sections.text: Documents include treaties, official reports, speeches and archives. Ask who wrote a document, for what purpose, and whether it is primary or secondary. Interviews can reveal reasons and experiences, but memory and position shape answers. Triangulation means checking a claim against two or more independent sources. Reliable sources include official records, peer-reviewed articles and named experts. Anonymous claims are weaker unless they can be checked.

sections.heading: Numbers, cause and ethics
sections.text: Quantitative data are numbers such as counts, rates or survey answers. A correlation means two things move together. Causation means one thing changes another. To argue causation, rule out reverse causation and confounding. Research ethics require informed consent, privacy, avoiding harm and honesty about limits. A student should record every source so others can check the work.

keyPoints: A concept becomes measurable through operationalisation, which turns it into a variable.
A case study examines one unit in depth; comparison tests an argument across two or more cases.
Confounding variables and selection bias can make a comparison misleading.
Documents and interviews are evidence, but their origin and purpose must be checked.
Correlation is not causation; causal claims must rule out reverse causation and confounding.
Research ethics require informed consent, privacy, avoiding harm and honest recording of sources.

en.title: Realism and Neorealism
en.short: Classical realism, neorealism, anarchy, self-help, balancing, the security dilemma and main criticisms.

sections.heading: Classical realism
sections.text:
Classical realism explains international politics through human nature. It is associated with Thucydides, Machiavelli, Hobbes and Hans Morgenthau. Morgenthau argued that people seek power, and that statesmen pursue the national interest defined as power. Politics is therefore a struggle for advantage, and morality cannot be applied to states as it is to individuals.

This realism is pessimistic about progress. It expects conflict because the desire for power is rooted in people, not only in the system. It advises leaders to think in terms of interests, not crusades.

sections.heading: Neorealism
sections.text:
Kenneth Waltz’s neorealism, or structural realism, moves the explanation to the structure of the international system. Structure means the arrangement of units and the distribution of capabilities. Because there is no world government, the system is anarchic. Anarchy does not mean chaos; it means no central authority above states.

States are sovereign and formally equal. They must rely on themselves for security, so self-help is the rule. Their first goal is survival. Power is a means to security, not always an end.

sections.heading: Core concepts
sections.text:
Balancing is a response to threat. States balance internally by arming and externally by allying. The security dilemma arises when one state’s defensive steps look offensive to others. Each reacts, so both become less secure.

Suppose two neighbouring states, Kanda and Mire, in an African region. Kanda buys tanks to defend its border. Mire sees the tanks as preparation for attack, so it buys tanks too. Kanda feels less safe. Neither wanted war, but the arms race makes war more likely.

sections.heading: Criticisms
sections.text:
Critics say realism is state-centric and ignores domestic politics, norms, law and institutions. It struggles to explain cooperation and change. Neorealism is also called too structural and deterministic: it predicts balancing, yet states sometimes join the stronger side (bandwagon) or fail to balance.

Realists reply that anarchy and self-help remain basic constraints. Liberalism and constructivism offer different answers, but realism remains a starting point for thinking about power and security.

keyPoints: Classical realism explains conflict by human nature and the pursuit of power.
Neorealism explains it by the anarchic structure of the international system.
Anarchy means no central world government, so states must practise self-help.
Survival is the primary goal, and balancing is a common response to threat.
The security dilemma shows how defensive measures can trigger an arms race.
Critics say realism ignores domestic politics, norms, institutions and change, while realists reply that anarchy remains a basic constraint.

en.title: Liberalism and Neoliberal Institutionalism
en.short: Liberal cooperation, regimes, Keohane, absolute gains, and realist and critical objections.

sections.heading: Liberal foundations
sections.text: Liberal thought holds that war is not inevitable. Trade raises the cost of conflict, and domestic institutions such as parliaments and courts can constrain leaders. The democratic peace thesis claims that democracies rarely fight one another, though scholars debate why. Liberals also stress international law and organisations as ways to settle disputes. They expect states to seek absolute gains, meaning gains measured without comparing them to other states’ gains. Liberals disagree about how far law can bind states, but they share a belief that institutions can change behaviour over time.

sections.heading: Neoliberal institutionalism
sections.text: Neoliberal institutionalism accepts anarchy, meaning the absence of a central world government, not chaos. It asks how states still cooperate. A regime is a set of principles, norms, rules and decision-making procedures around which expectations converge in a given issue area. Robert Keohane argues that institutions reduce transaction costs, share information, monitor compliance and make promises credible. Repeated interaction and issue linkage raise the cost of cheating. Institutions do not force states; they change incentives. They can also pool authority or delegate tasks, as in courts and secretariats.

sections.heading: Objections
sections.text: Realists object that institutions reflect state power and do little when security is at stake. States worry about relative gains and cheating, so cooperation is fragile. Critical scholars argue that regimes can encode Western or neoliberal preferences, favour strong states and exclude weaker voices. Legitimacy and distributive bias therefore matter. They also ask who is recognised as a legitimate participant.

sections.heading: Concrete case
sections.text: In the World Trade Organization, members use dispute settlement panels to rule on trade complaints, and appeals used to go to the Appellate Body. This lowers uncertainty and sets rules for retaliation. Yet the system depends on member power and political will. The United States has blocked new Appellate Body appointments, leaving appeals unresolved and weakening cooperation.

keyPoints: Liberals argue that trade, domestic institutions and international law can make cooperation more likely.
Neoliberal institutionalism says regimes and organisations help states cooperate under anarchy by reducing costs, sharing information and monitoring compliance.
Realists reply that institutions reflect power and are weak when relative gains and security dominate.
Critical scholars stress that institutions can have distributive bias and exclude weaker states.
The WTO dispute settlement case shows both institutional cooperation and its dependence on political will.

en.title: Constructivism, Identity and Norms
en.short: How shared ideas, identities and norms shape state interests, and how constructivists study change.

sections.heading: Social construction
sections.text:
Constructivism holds that international reality is socially constructed. Many facts exist because people collectively believe and act on them. A border post or a currency is a social fact: it works only while officials and citizens recognise it.

Alexander Wendt argued in 1992 that anarchy is what states make of it. Anarchy does not by itself create self-help. States’ identities, formed in interaction, shape whether they see each other as rivals, partners or threats. Identities are understandings of who an actor is. They create interests: a state that sees itself as a responsible power may want different things from one that sees itself as a victim.

sections.heading: Norms and change
sections.text:
Norms are shared expectations about appropriate behaviour. Regulative norms constrain what actors do. Constitutive norms define who counts as an actor and what its interests are. Constructivists argue that actors often follow a logic of appropriateness: they ask what a person like me should do, not only what pays.

Norms change through persuasion and social pressure. Finnemore and Sikkink describe a norm life cycle: emergence, when norm entrepreneurs campaign; cascade, when many states adopt the norm; and internalisation, when it becomes taken for granted. The African Union’s norm against unconstitutional changes of government, written into its Constitutive Act, has led to suspensions after coups, though enforcement is uneven.

sections.heading: Agent, structure and criticism
sections.text:
The agent-structure problem asks how much to explain by actors and how much by the social structure around them. Constructivists say the two are mutually constituted. Structures of shared norms shape agents, and agents reproduce or change those structures.

This helps explain change, but it brings criticisms. Constructivism can be vague about how to measure identities and norms. It can be hard to test, because norms and interests may be defined in ways that fit any evidence. Critics say it sometimes ignores material power and treats norms as more stable than they are. Others reply that material power itself needs shared meanings to matter.

keyPoints: Constructivism treats international reality as socially constructed through shared beliefs and practices.
Identities define who actors are and shape their interests.
Norms are shared expectations of appropriate behaviour; regulative norms constrain and constitutive norms define actors.
The agent-structure problem is central: agents and structures are mutually constituted.
Finnemore and Sikkink’s norm life cycle describes emergence, cascade and internalisation.
Critics say constructivism can be vague, hard to test, and may underplay material power.

en.title: Critical, Feminist and Postcolonial Approaches to IR
en.short: Marxist, feminist, postcolonial and green critiques of mainstream International Relations.

sections.heading: Critical starting points
sections.text:
Critical approaches ask whose power mainstream International Relations (IR) hides. Mainstream IR often takes states, markets and security as given and treats them as neutral.

Critical scholars say these categories are social and historical, and they serve some groups more than others. They also question the claim that IR can be objective and free of politics. The four approaches below share that suspicion but not one programme.

sections.heading: Class and empire
sections.text:
Marxist IR starts from class and capitalism. It sees global politics as shaped by the accumulation of capital, not only by states. Richer core states and firms gain from unequal exchange with poorer regions.

Feminism starts from gender: the social meanings given to men and women. It shows how security, war and diplomacy are coded masculine, while women’s labour and peace work are often ignored. Postcolonial IR starts from empire. It argues that colonial rule and Eurocentrism, the habit of treating European experience as universal, still structure knowledge and power, so the “international” is not a level field.

sections.heading: Gender and ecology
sections.text:
Green or ecological IR starts from the biosphere. It says mainstream accounts treat nature as a free resource and ignore ecological limits and non-human life.

These approaches disagree. Marxists stress class and production; feminists reply that gender and unpaid care cannot be reduced to class. Postcolonial scholars criticise both Marxism and feminism for speaking from the West. Feminists and postcolonial scholars also argue over whether “women” is a universal category. Greens say the others remain human-centred.

sections.heading: Niger Delta case
sections.text:
In the Niger Delta, Nigeria, oil extraction has produced revenue, pollution and conflict.

A Marxist reading stresses capital and unequal benefit sharing. A postcolonial reading stresses colonial extraction and the marginalisation of local communities. A feminist reading asks who fetches water and who bears pollution. A green reading stresses damaged ecosystems. Each reveals something, and each misses what the others see.

keyPoints: Critical approaches ask whose interests mainstream IR serves and treat its categories as historical.
Marxist IR explains global politics through class, capitalism and unequal exchange.
Feminist IR shows how gender shapes security, war, diplomacy and political economy.
Postcolonial IR traces how empire and Eurocentrism continue to shape knowledge and power.
Green IR places ecological limits and non-human life at the centre.
The approaches disagree over whether class, gender, empire or ecology is the main axis of power.

en.title: Foreign Policy Analysis
en.short: How states decide foreign policy: rational actor, bureaucratic politics, domestic and international limits.

sections.heading: What FPA studies
sections.text:
Foreign policy is the set of goals and actions by which a state deals with other states and other international actors. Foreign policy analysis (FPA) asks how those decisions are made: who decides, and within what limits.

It differs from systemic IR theory, which explains outcomes from the structure of the international system. Systemic theory treats the state as one unit; FPA opens the state up. The two are complements: structure sets the room to manoeuvre, FPA explains the choice made inside it.

sections.heading: The rational actor model
sections.text:
Graham Allison’s Essence of Decision (1971) calls this Model I, the rational actor. The state acts as one purposive decision-maker: it sets goals, lists options, weighs costs and benefits, and picks the best.

It is a useful baseline, because it predicts that a state will answer threats and incentives. Its weakness is that it assumes a single mind with full information, so it cannot explain incoherent policy or a policy that serves one ministry’s interest.

sections.heading: Bureaucratic politics
sections.text:
Allison’s Model III, bureaucratic politics, sees policy as a bargain among officials whose posts give them different interests: where you stand depends on where you sit. Model II, organisational process, adds that the routines of ministries and armed forces shape the options that reach leaders.

Illustrative case: a state negotiating a foreign loan. The finance ministry accepts the lender’s terms, the trade ministry fears the tariff cuts, the foreign ministry wants to keep a regional ally. The package finally agreed is a compromise none of them designed.

sections.heading: Domestic and international limits
sections.text:
Leaders answer to parliaments, parties, media, voters and interest groups. Robert Putnam (1988) described two-level games: a negotiator must satisfy both the foreign counterpart and the home constituency, and a narrow win-set, meaning the range of deals the home side would accept, can strengthen the negotiator’s hand.

Public opinion usually constrains rather than commands, and matters most on visible issues. International pressure, through sanctions, aid conditions, alliances and markets, marks the outer limits.

keyPoints: Foreign policy analysis explains how states decide; systemic theory explains why outcomes are patterned by international structure.
The rational actor model treats the state as one purposive decision-maker weighing options against goals.
Bureaucratic politics sees policy as bargaining among officials whose positions shape their preferences.
Organisational process stresses that standard routines limit the options leaders receive.
Putnam’s two-level game shows leaders answering to domestic and foreign audiences at once.
Public opinion and international pressure usually constrain choices rather than dictate them.

en.title: Diplomacy and Negotiation: Representation, Bargaining and Mediation
en.short: How diplomats represent states in embassies and conferences, and how negotiation, bargaining and mediation work.

sections.heading: The work of diplomacy
sections.text: Diplomacy is the conduct of relations between states and other international actors through official representatives. A bilateral embassy is a permanent mission in another country, led by an ambassador accredited to that state. It reports, protects citizens, explains policy and builds contacts. A consulate handles practical matters such as visas and help to nationals. Multilateral diplomacy works through conferences and organisations, where many states negotiate texts, rules and declarations. Delegates need instructions, coordination and skill in drafting, because wording can decide obligations.

sections.heading: Negotiation stages
sections.text: Negotiation usually moves through preparation, opening, bargaining, closing and implementation. Preparation means defining interests, not only positions; a position is what a side says it wants, while an interest is the underlying need. Negotiators gather facts, set priorities, imagine the other side’s concerns and agree a fallback. Opening sets the agenda and tone. Bargaining exchanges proposals and concessions. Closing records what was accepted. Implementation checks that promises are kept. A simple case: two neighbouring states share a river. Upstream wants irrigation; downstream fears low flow. A fixed quota may fail if rainfall changes. A rule to share actual flow, with regular meetings, can manage uncertainty.

sections.heading: Bargaining and mediation
sections.text: Bargaining works best when both sides see gains. Integrative bargaining seeks joint gains, for example linking a water-sharing rule to funding for efficient irrigation. Distributive bargaining divides a fixed amount. Mediation is when a neutral third party helps the parties reach their own agreement; the mediator does not impose a decision. With good offices, a third party provides a channel or venue for talks without joining them; conciliation adds an inquiry and a non-binding proposed settlement; arbitration produces a binding decision. Mediators listen, clarify interests, separate people from problems and suggest options.

sections.heading: Ethics and preparation
sections.text: Professional ethics require a representative to act within instructions, report accurately, keep confidences and avoid private interests that conflict with the public role. A diplomat must not promise what the state has not authorised. Preparation includes clear communication: short briefs, active listening, cultural awareness and written records. In conferences, check the mandate, deadlines and decision rule before speaking.

keyPoints: Diplomacy is official representation and communication between states and other international actors.
Bilateral diplomacy uses embassies and consulates; multilateral diplomacy uses conferences and organisations.
Negotiation stages are preparation, opening, bargaining, closing and implementation.
Positions are stated demands; interests are underlying needs, and interest-based bargaining can create joint gains.
Mediation is third-party help without a binding decision; arbitration imposes a decision.
Ethical representation requires following instructions, accurate reporting, confidentiality and avoiding conflicts of interest.

en.title: International Security and Strategy: Force, Deterrence and Restraint
en.short: Strategy, deterrence, alliances, arms control, changing war, intervention and the law of force.

sections.heading: Strategy and deterrence
sections.text: Strategy is the linking of political ends to military means. A strategy sets objectives, chooses ways (how force is used) and allocates means (troops, ships, money). Deterrence tries to stop an action by making its cost exceed its gain. It works through capability, credibility and communication. Punishment deterrence threatens retaliation; denial deterrence blocks the attack. Nuclear deterrence rests on the fear of unacceptable retaliation. Mutual assured destruction (MAD) is the condition in which each side can destroy the other after a first strike. It is a condition, not a policy, and it is unstable if leaders doubt second-strike survival.

sections.heading: Alliances and arms control
sections.text: Alliances pool capabilities and promise support. They can deter by showing that an attack will meet several states, not one. NATO is a collective defence alliance; its Article 5 treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all. Alliances manage allies, share burdens and signal resolve. Arms control limits weapons by treaty or informal rule. It can cap numbers, ban classes of weapon, or build transparency through inspections. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) rests on three pillars: non-proliferation, disarmament and peaceful use. Arms control does not abolish distrust; it makes military competition more predictable and less accident-prone.

sections.heading: Changing character
sections.text: War now mixes regular forces with insurgents, cyber attacks, drones and private military companies. Civil wars draw in neighbours and outside powers. Intervention may be unilateral or authorised by the UN Security Council under Chapter VII. Consent of the host state matters, but it can be withdrawn.

sections.heading: Law and ethics
sections.text: The UN Charter bans the threat or use of force except in self-defence or with Security Council authorisation. The laws of armed conflict require distinction between combatants and civilians, proportionality, precaution and military necessity. Ethical debate asks when intervention to stop atrocities is justified. In 1990, ECOWAS sent ECOMOG into Liberia’s civil war without Security Council authorisation; the UN later supported the peace process. It shows why legal authority and consent remain contested.

keyPoints: Strategy links political ends to military ways and means.
Deterrence works through capability, credibility and communication; it can punish or deny.
Alliances pool power and can deter through collective defence, as NATO’s Article 5 shows.
Arms control limits weapons and builds transparency but does not remove distrust.
Modern war mixes regular forces with insurgents, cyber, drones and private military companies.
Force is lawful only in self-defence or with Security Council authorisation, and the laws of armed conflict protect civilians.

en.title: Conflict Resolution and Peacebuilding
en.short: Conflict causes and stages, negotiation, mediation, peacekeeping, peacebuilding and local actors.

sections.heading: Causes and stages
sections.text:
Conflict is a disagreement between parties who perceive their goals as incompatible. Causes are often divided into structural and proximate. Structural causes include exclusion from power, inequality, weak institutions and competition over land or resources. Proximate causes are triggers such as a disputed election, a killing or a price shock. Grievances and the incentives of leaders both matter.

Stage models commonly describe latent conflict, escalation, crisis, de-escalation, settlement and post-conflict recovery. They are guides, not laws: conflicts can stall, relapse or skip stages.

sections.heading: Negotiation and mediation
sections.text:
Negotiation is direct communication between parties to reach an agreement. Mediation adds an acceptable third party who helps them communicate, clarify interests and save face, but does not impose a decision. Mediators need consent, leverage and context knowledge.

Mozambique’s civil war ended with the 1992 Rome General Peace Accords, mediated with the Community of Sant’Egidio and other actors. The UN operation ONUMOZ then monitored the ceasefire and supported elections. Mediation helped, but implementation depended on political will.

sections.heading: Peacekeeping and peacebuilding
sections.text:
Peacekeeping is the deployment of third-party personnel, often military and police, to monitor ceasefires, separate forces and protect civilians. UN peacekeeping traditionally rests on consent, impartiality and non-use of force except in self-defence and defence of the mandate, though some missions are authorised to use force more robustly.

Peacebuilding is longer-term work to address root causes: rebuilding institutions, justice, reconciliation, livelihoods and security. It is wider than peacekeeping and continues after troops leave.

sections.heading: Liberal peacebuilding debate
sections.text:
Liberal peacebuilding promotes democracy, market economies, human rights and civil society after war. Defenders say rights and accountable institutions are necessary for lasting peace. Critics argue that rapid elections can harden divisions and that external models may ignore local context.

The local turn stresses local ownership, hybrid arrangements and everyday peace. It warns against treating local actors as either victims or peacemakers. Local elites can capture processes, and local practices can be exclusionary. The debate is not settled: external support can help, but legitimacy usually depends on local consent.

keyPoints: Conflict has structural causes and proximate triggers; stage models are guides, not fixed laws.
Negotiation is direct bargaining; mediation adds a third party but leaves the decision with the parties.
Peacekeeping monitors ceasefires and protects civilians, usually with consent; peacebuilding addresses root causes over years.
Liberal peacebuilding promotes elections, markets and rights, but critics say it can ignore local context.
Local ownership and hybrid peace can increase legitimacy, but local actors are not automatically peaceful.
Mozambique’s Rome Accords and ONUMOZ show mediation and peacekeeping can support a settlement, though peacebuilding continues.

en.title: International Organisations and Global Governance
en.short: Why states build international organisations, how the UN works, and the promise and limits of global governance.

sections.heading: Why states create them
sections.text: States create international organisations (IOs) because some problems cross borders and cannot be solved by one government alone. Security, trade, health, transport and the environment all need coordination. An IO is a formal body with member states, rules and a secretariat. It lowers the cost of bargaining, pools information, makes promises more credible and lets states monitor one another. States delegate some authority but normally keep control through voting rules, budgets and withdrawal. Realists expect IOs to reflect powerful states, liberals stress shared gains, and constructivists stress norms and identities.

sections.heading: How the UN works
sections.text:
The United Nations was founded in 1945. Its Charter gives different powers to different organs. The General Assembly has one state, one vote and mainly adopts non-binding recommendations. The Security Council has primary responsibility for peace and security. It has five permanent members, China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, each with a veto, plus elected members. The Secretariat, led by the Secretary-General, administers the organisation. Specialised agencies such as the World Health Organization and the International Labour Organization are separate bodies linked to the UN.

The veto shows how rules shape outcomes. A Security Council resolution needs nine affirmative votes and no negative vote from a permanent member. If one permanent member votes no, the resolution fails even if the other fourteen members support it. This protects great-power interests but can block collective action.

sections.heading: Regimes and governance
sections.text: A regime is a set of principles, norms, rules and decision-making procedures around an issue area. Global governance is the wider sum of formal and informal institutions and rules that manage cross-border problems. It is not world government. Legitimacy is acceptance that an institution has the right to make rules. Effectiveness is whether it achieves its stated goals. An institution can be legitimate but ineffective, or effective but weakly legitimate. The main limits are sovereignty, free riding (enjoying benefits without sharing costs), vetoes, weak enforcement, funding and disagreement over goals.

keyPoints: States create international organisations to reduce bargaining costs, make commitments credible and monitor shared problems.
The UN Charter divides authority among the General Assembly, Security Council, Secretariat and other organs.
A regime is a set of principles, norms, rules and decision procedures around an issue area.
Global governance is the formal and informal rules that manage cross-border problems, not world government.
Legitimacy is acceptance of an institution’s authority; effectiveness is whether it meets its goals.
Limits include sovereignty, free riding, vetoes, weak enforcement, funding and disagreement over goals.

en.title: International Law and Human Rights
en.short: Sources of international law, courts, human rights systems, state responsibility and sovereignty tensions.

sections.heading: Sources and making
sections.text:
International law is made by states. Article 38(1) of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) Statute lists treaties, custom and general principles, with judicial decisions and writings as subsidiary means. A treaty is an agreement between states, governed by the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969). It binds a state after ratification, and pacta sunt servanda means agreements must be kept. Reservations can exclude or modify parts if compatible with the treaty’s object and purpose.

Custom needs two elements: widespread and consistent state practice, and opinio juris, the belief that the practice is legally required. A persistent objector can escape a new custom. General principles fill gaps, such as good faith.

sections.heading: Courts and human rights
sections.text:
The human rights system began with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), not itself a treaty. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) (1966) made many rights binding; treaty bodies monitor them, and regional systems hear complaints.

Courts apply law but rarely enforce it. The ICJ hears state disputes with consent. The International Criminal Court tries individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression. In Social and Economic Rights Action Center v Nigeria (2001), the African Commission found Nigeria responsible for oil pollution in Ogoniland harming health, environment and livelihood. A state can breach rights by failing to protect people from private companies.

sections.heading: State responsibility and sovereignty
sections.text:
State responsibility concerns breaches. Under the International Law Commission’s Articles on State Responsibility (2001), conduct attributable to a state that breaches an international obligation is a wrongful act. The state must stop and make reparation: restitution, compensation or satisfaction.

Human rights challenge sovereignty. Sovereignty means legal independence and non-interference, but human rights treaties limit how a state treats its own people. Enforcement remains weak because states consent to courts and powerful states resist scrutiny. Universal rights are proclaimed, yet implementation depends on state will and regional institutions.

keyPoints: Treaties, custom and general principles are the main sources of international law.
Custom requires state practice plus opinio juris.
The ICJ hears state disputes only with consent; the ICC tries individuals.
State responsibility requires a breach attributable to a state, and reparation follows.
Human rights treaties limit sovereignty, but enforcement depends on state consent.
Social and Economic Rights Action Center v Nigeria shows responsibility for failing to protect people from private harm.

en.title: Global Trade, Finance and Multinational Corporations
en.short: Trade liberalisation debates, global finance, FDI and how institutions and firms shape state choices.

sections.heading: Trade: free or protected?
sections.text: Trade liberalisation means lowering tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (quantity limits) and other barriers. The case for it rests on comparative advantage: countries gain by specialising where opportunity cost is lower. The case against includes infant-industry protection, food security, revenue and defence. Distributive effects matter: consumers and exporters usually gain, while import-competing producers and workers may lose. The World Trade Organization (WTO), created in 1995, sets rules and hears disputes, but enforcement is slow and unequal. Example: a 20% tariff on an imported machine costing 1,000 raises its price to 1,200, helping local producers but taxing buyers.

sections.heading: Finance and policy space
sections.text: Global finance means cross-border lending, investment and currency exchange. Capital mobility can fund growth, but sudden stops (abrupt halts in capital inflows) and currency crises can force governments to cut spending. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) lends to states in balance-of-payments trouble, often with conditions such as fiscal discipline and structural reform. Supporters say conditions restore confidence; critics say they shrink policy space and shift adjustment costs onto wages and public services. Exchange-rate choices (fixed, floating or managed) also distribute gains and losses between exporters, importers, debtors and creditors. Capital controls may slow outflows but can raise borrowing costs. These trade-offs vary by country and period, so check current IMF rules and national law.

sections.heading: Multinational firms and FDI
sections.text: Foreign direct investment (FDI) is a firm’s lasting ownership or control of assets in another country. Multinational corporations (MNCs) use FDI to access markets, resources and cheaper labour. They shape state choices through investment incentives, tax competition, lobbying and threats to relocate. Gains include jobs, technology transfer and tax revenue. Costs include profit repatriation (profits sent home rather than reinvested locally), transfer pricing (pricing deals between affiliates to shift profits into low-tax countries), weak labour or environmental standards and few local linkages. Case: a government offers Copperline Ltd a ten-year tax holiday to build a plant. If expected tax is 5 million a year, forgone revenue is 50 million. The plant may still be worth it, but the bargain should be published and reviewed.

keyPoints: Trade liberalisation lowers tariffs and quotas, but gains and losses are unevenly distributed.
Comparative advantage explains gains from trade; infant-industry and security arguments justify protection.
The WTO sets trade rules and settles disputes, but enforcement is uneven.
Global finance can fund growth, but crises and IMF conditionality can reduce policy space.
FDI brings jobs and technology but may bring profit repatriation and transfer pricing.
MNCs shape state choices through incentives, tax competition and relocation threats.

en.title: Development and Global Inequality
en.short: Contested meanings of development, aid, debt, trade rules and mainstream versus critical views of inequality.

sections.heading: Meanings of development
sections.text: Development is contested. Mainstream economics often means rising income per person and structural change from farming to industry. The human development approach, associated with Amartya Sen and the UNDP, asks what people can actually do and be: health, education, freedoms. Sustainable development adds environmental limits. Critical accounts ask how underdevelopment is produced. Dependency and world-systems writers argue that colonial extraction and unequal exchange keep poorer countries supplying cheap primary goods and buying expensive manufactures. Postcolonial scholars add that ideas of 'progress’ carry power; feminist scholars ask who bears unpaid care work.

sections.heading: Aid, debt and trade
sections.text: Official development assistance (ODA) is public aid on softer terms than market loans. Mainstream debates ask whether aid raises investment when institutions are accountable; critics stress conditionality (conditions attached to aid), donor priorities and aid dependency. Sovereign debt can force austerity; debt relief such as the HIPC Initiative links relief to poverty plans. The WTO allows special and differential treatment for developing members, but critics point to tariff escalation, which taxes processed goods more than raw materials, and farm subsidies in rich countries.

sections.heading: A concrete case
sections.text: Imagine Kanda, a fictional small African economy. It exports raw cocoa and imports chocolate. Tariff escalation discourages local processing, so most value is captured abroad. A foreign loan builds a port, but conditions require privatisation and spending cuts. When cocoa prices fall, debt service competes with schools. Aid may build clinics, yet if donors choose the projects, Kanda’s ownership is weak. The case shows how these interact.

sections.heading: Mainstream and critical
sections.text: Mainstream accounts emphasise growth, open markets, good institutions and targeted aid. Critical accounts reply that unequal power in trade, finance and knowledge reproduces inequality, so redistribution and policy space matter. Global inequality is measured between and within countries. Neither side has a monopoly: East Asian industrial policy and commodity booms show states can shape development, while corruption and conflict can defeat aid. Students should check current figures with the World Bank, IMF, UNDP or WTO, because classifications and rules change.

keyPoints: Development is contested: growth, human development, sustainable development and structural change are different criteria.
Dependency and world-systems accounts treat underdevelopment as produced by colonial and unequal global economic relations, not as a simple lag.
Aid debates centre on effectiveness, conditionality, ownership and dependency; ODA is public finance on softer than market terms.
Sovereign debt crises can force austerity, and debt relief initiatives such as HIPC link relief to poverty-reduction plans.
Trade rules can help or hinder development: special and differential treatment offers flexibility, while tariff escalation and rich-country subsidies can keep value added abroad.
Mainstream accounts stress growth, institutions and open markets; critical accounts stress power, redistribution and policy space.

en.title: Regional Integration and African Institutions
en.short: Theories of regional integration, the AU and ECOWAS, and their security, trade and governance roles.

sections.heading: Theories of integration
sections.text: Regional integration is when states pool rules, markets or authority in a region. Functionalism (David Mitrany) expects cooperation on technical problems such as transport or health to build peace. Neofunctionalism (Ernst Haas) adds spillover: integration in one sector creates pressure to integrate neighbouring sectors. Intergovernmentalism (Stanley Hoffmann) replies that states control the pace and keep sovereignty where they value it. Liberal intergovernmentalism (Andrew Moravcsik) explains integration as a bargain among states shaped by domestic interests and credible commitments.

sections.heading: African Union
sections.text: The African Union (AU), created in 2002, replaced the Organisation of African Unity. It has 55 member states and pursues political and economic integration. Its Peace and Security Council decides on responses to conflict, supported by the African Standby Force, which is still not fully operational. Article 4(h) of the AU Constitutive Act permits intervention in grave cases such as genocide, if the Assembly agrees. The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is an AU trade treaty, and the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance sets governance standards.

sections.heading: ECOWAS
sections.text: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was founded in 1975 by the Treaty of Lagos, with a revised treaty in 1993. It promotes trade liberalisation, a common external tariff and free movement. Its 2001 Protocol on Democracy and Good Governance sets rules on elections and coups. In security, ECOWAS deployed ECOMOG (the ECOWAS Monitoring Group) to Liberia in 1990 to monitor a ceasefire; the mission became a peace enforcement operation, though critics said it was dominated by Nigeria.

sections.heading: Problems faced
sections.text: Regional bodies face weak enforcement, limited funds and dependence on external donors. Sovereignty makes members resist binding rules, and overlapping membership in the AU, ECOWAS and other communities duplicates effort. Coups and disputed elections test governance rules, and sanctions can hurt ordinary people. Security missions may lack troops, money or neutral command. Integration can also be uneven, with stronger states gaining more. These problems do not make regional integration useless, but they show why African institutions often act slowly.

keyPoints: Neofunctionalism expects spillover, while intergovernmentalism stresses state bargains.
The AU replaced the OAU in 2002 and has 55 member states.
Article 4(h) of the AU Constitutive Act allows intervention in grave cases such as genocide.
ECOWAS was founded in 1975 and promotes trade liberalisation, free movement and democratic governance.
ECOMOG in Liberia in 1990 shows ECOWAS security action and its command and neutrality problems.
African regional bodies are limited by weak enforcement, funding gaps, sovereignty and overlapping membership.

en.title: Environment, Climate Change and Global Governance
en.short: Transboundary harm, the commons, climate treaties, and disputes over equity and enforcement.

sections.heading: Why harm crosses borders
sections.text:
Environmental damage rarely stops at a border. A factory upstream pollutes a river that two countries share. Greenhouse gases released anywhere mix in the atmosphere and warm everywhere. Economists call the benefits of cutting emissions a public good: no one can be excluded from a stable climate, and one state’s cut benefits all. But the atmosphere’s capacity to absorb emissions is rival, so it is a common-pool resource, like fish stocks and shared rivers: hard to fence off.

Because no one owns the atmosphere, each state gains by letting others cut emissions while it does not. Garrett Hardin called this the tragedy of the commons (1968). Elinor Ostrom (1990) answered that communities often escape it through agreed rules, monitoring and sanctions. States try the same at global level.

sections.heading: Climate negotiations
sections.text:
States respond by building regimes: sets of principles, norms, rules and decision procedures around an issue. The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (1992) set the frame. The Kyoto Protocol (1997) bound rich countries to emission targets; the United States never ratified it and Canada later withdrew.

The Paris Agreement (2015) changed the method. Each state submits a nationally determined contribution (NDC) and reports progress. The aim is to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C. The targets are politically binding; the legal duties are reporting and review.

sections.heading: Equity and enforcement
sections.text:
Equity divides negotiators. The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, stated in the 1992 Rio Declaration, holds that rich states, which emitted most historically, should lead. India and many African states stress per capita emissions; small island states stress survival. This is the climate justice debate.

Enforcement is weak because no world government exists. The Montreal Protocol (1987) on ozone worked because cheap substitutes existed and a fund helped poorer states switch. Climate is harder, since fossil fuels underpin economies. Governance is now a regime complex: treaties, courts, investors and cities, not one hierarchy.

keyPoints: Cutting emissions is a public good, so states have incentives to free-ride.
Hardin’s tragedy of the commons is countered by Ostrom’s evidence on self-governance.
Kyoto set binding targets for rich states; Paris uses voluntary NDCs with binding reporting.
Common but differentiated responsibilities is the main equity principle in climate talks.
Enforcement is weak because there is no central authority above states.
Montreal succeeded through substitutes and a fund; climate faces harder economic trade-offs.

en.title: Transnational Security Threats: Cross-Border Risks and Responses
en.short: Terrorism, migration, organised crime, piracy and disease as cross-border threats; responses and rights tensions.

sections.heading: What makes a threat transnational
sections.text: Transnational security threats are harms that cross borders and involve non-state actors or flows, so no single state can manage them alone. Terrorism is politically motivated violence against civilians, intended to influence an audience; definitions vary and there is no universal legal definition. Migration is movement across borders. It is not a threat in itself, but irregular or forced migration can raise security, humanitarian and border-control concerns. Organised crime is planned illegal activity by groups for profit, often trafficking drugs, arms or people and laundering money. Piracy is violent theft or detention at sea for private ends; under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea it occurs on the high seas. Disease outbreaks spread through travel and trade.

sections.heading: How states respond
sections.text: States respond with border controls, intelligence sharing, police and judicial cooperation, naval patrols and public health surveillance. International bodies coordinate. The UN Security Council and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime address terrorism and organised crime; Interpol supports policing; the World Health Organization uses the International Health Regulations (2005) for disease. Regional bodies such as the African Union and ECOWAS also act. Treaties matter, for example the Palermo Convention against Transnational Organized Crime (2000). Responses may be legal, diplomatic, military or public health measures.

sections.heading: Security, rights and cooperation
sections.text: Strong responses can clash with rights. Counterterrorism surveillance may invade privacy; migration detention may breach refugee protection; piracy trials raise fair-trial questions; quarantine limits movement. Cooperation also clashes with sovereignty, because states resist foreign scrutiny and intelligence sharing. Effective policy needs proportionality, legality and accountability. In the 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, the WHO declared a public health emergency and states screened travellers. Some border closures slowed trade and harmed livelihoods, showing the tension between containment, rights and cooperation.

keyPoints: Transnational threats cross borders and involve non-state actors or flows, so they need cooperation between states.
Terrorism has no universally agreed legal definition, which complicates international action.
Migration is not a threat in itself; security concerns arise from irregular or forced movement and from state responses.
Organised crime and piracy are profit-driven illegal activities that cross borders and require police, judicial and naval cooperation.
Disease control depends on surveillance and the WHO International Health Regulations (2005).
Counterterrorism, migration control and quarantine can conflict with rights, so responses need legality and proportionality.

en.title: Research Design and Data in International Relations
en.short: Framing questions, selecting and comparing cases, using data, and judging validity, reliability, bias and ethics.

sections.heading: From puzzle to question
