sections.text: A research question asks what relationship you will explain, not just what topic you will describe. It should be answerable with evidence, narrow enough for the time available, and linked to a debate. State the dependent variable (the outcome to explain) and the independent variable (the suspected cause). For example: do peacekeeping missions with civilian-protection mandates reduce civilian killings? Define key terms and say what evidence would count for or against.

sections.heading: Choosing cases
sections.text: Case selection is strategic, not random. In a most similar systems design, cases share many features but differ on the outcome and suspected cause. In a most different systems design, cases differ widely but share the outcome. A single case can test a theory through process tracing, which traces the chain between cause and effect. Avoid selecting only cases that confirm your argument; include hard cases or outliers where possible.

sections.heading: Data and comparison
sections.text: Qualitative data include documents, interviews, speeches and archives; quantitative data are numbers such as battle deaths, trade flows or vote shares. Comparison can be small-N (few cases, deep analysis) or large-N (many cases, statistical analysis). Operationalisation is turning a concept into measurable indicators. If two coders classify 50 reports and agree on 40, simple agreement is 40 ÷ 50 = 0.80, or 80 per cent. That is one check on reliability.

sections.heading: Validity, bias, ethics
sections.text: Validity means measuring the right concept; reliability means getting consistent results on repetition. Internal validity concerns whether the design supports a causal claim; external validity concerns whether findings travel to other cases. Bias can enter through case selection, missing data or the researcher’s expectations. Ethics require informed consent, confidentiality, no harm to participants, and honesty about sources and limits. Check official data sources and state their dates and definitions.

keyPoints: A good research question names an outcome and a suspected cause and can be answered with evidence.
Case selection should follow the logic of the research question, not convenience alone.
Most similar and most different designs compare cases to control for alternative explanations.
Qualitative data support process tracing; quantitative data support large-N comparison.
Validity asks whether you measure the right concept; reliability asks whether results repeat, and simple agreement = agreements ÷ total items.
Ethical research protects participants and reports sources, limits and possible bias honestly.

en.title: Advanced International Relations Theory
en.short: Meta-theory, ontology, epistemology, explanation, agent-structure and four IR traditions compared.

sections.heading: Meta-theory: three questions
sections.text: Meta-theory asks what a theory assumes before it explains. Ontology is what exists: states, classes, individuals or ideas. Epistemology is how we know: observable evidence, interpretation of meaning, or critique of power. Explanation is what counts as an answer: a causal law, a constitutive rule, or an emancipatory diagnosis. Positivists seek testable causal regularities; post-positivists, often called reflectivists, argue that social reality is meaningful and knowledge is not neutral.

sections.heading: Comparing the traditions
sections.text: Realism and liberalism are rationalist: actors calculate means to ends. Realism has a materialist ontology, with anarchy and capabilities driving states. Liberalism adds institutions, domestic politics and interdependence. Constructivism has a social ontology: norms and identities constitute actors and interests, so explanation is often constitutive. Critical approaches ask how knowledge and power produce exclusion, and favour critique over neutral prediction. The traditions disagree about what needs explaining and what counts as an explanation.

sections.heading: Agent and structure
sections.text: The agent-structure problem asks whether actors or structures explain outcomes. Kenneth Waltz made structure central, but critics said his states were undifferentiated units. Alexander Wendt argued that agents and structures are mutually constitutive: states create anarchy through shared ideas, and anarchy shapes identities. Anthony Giddens’s structuration theory says structures enable and constrain action, while action reproduces structure. In a hypothetical West African state deciding whether to obey a regional court, realism stresses sovereignty, liberalism reputation, constructivism legal obligation, and critical theory whose interests the court serves.

sections.heading: Eclecticism and limits
sections.text: Eclecticism combines insights from different theories. Analytic eclecticism, associated with Rudra Sil and Peter Katzenstein, uses mechanisms from several traditions without claiming one grand theory. The danger is incommensurability: theories rest on different ontologies and epistemologies, so mixing can become ad hoc. A good eclectic argument states which assumptions it borrows and why they fit. For the court case, it might combine realist sovereignty costs, liberal reputation and constructivist norm internalisation, while saying which mechanism dominates when.

keyPoints: Ontology asks what exists, epistemology asks how we can know, and explanation asks what counts as a good answer.
Realism and liberalism are broadly rationalist, but realism stresses material capabilities while liberalism adds institutions and domestic politics.
Constructivism treats norms and identities as constitutive of actors and interests, not merely as causal variables.
Critical approaches connect knowledge to power and ask who is excluded by prevailing theories and practices.
The agent-structure problem asks whether actors or structures explain outcomes; Wendt and Giddens stress their mutual constitution.
Eclecticism can enrich explanation, but it risks incommensurability unless the borrowed assumptions are made explicit.

en.title: Advanced Research Methods and the Dissertation
en.short: Designing a master’s dissertation: question, literature, case selection, inference, ethics and defence.

sections.heading: From literature to question
sections.text:
A dissertation starts with the literature, not the topic. Read until you can state the main debate in your field and what each side claims. A literature review is an argument, not a list: it shows what is settled, what is contested and what has been missed. That gap becomes your question.

A good master’s question names the outcome, the cases and the period, and is phrased so evidence could prove it wrong. 'Why do some regional bodies enforce decisions and others not?' is a question; 'a study of regional bodies’ is not.

sections.heading: Cases and causal inference
sections.text:
Case selection follows the question. To test a theory, pick cases where it should hold and cases where it should fail. A most similar design compares cases alike in background but different in outcome; a most different design does the reverse. Never select only cases where the outcome happened: without variation you cannot see what caused it.

Process tracing follows the mechanism inside one case, using documents and interviews. Quantitative methods compare many cases with variables and statistics. Both face confounding, where a third factor drives both cause and effect, so always ask what the counterfactual is: what would have happened without the cause.

A student asks why two states ratified an African Union protocol quickly and two did not; she pairs them by regime type and income, then traces ministry files.

sections.heading: Ethics, data and defence
sections.text:
Ethics approval comes before fieldwork. Seek informed consent, protect identities where disclosure could harm people, and never promise confidentiality you cannot keep. Rules differ by country and institution, so check your committee’s procedure.

Manage data from day one: a data management plan records files, versions, backups and access, and an audit trail lets others retrace your steps.

A defensible argument states a claim, gives evidence and shows the warrant linking them, then answers the strongest objection. Plan backwards from the deadline.

keyPoints: A literature review is an argument that locates a gap, not a summary of everything read.
A research question should name the outcome, the cases and the period, and be falsifiable.
Case selection must produce variation in the outcome; choosing only positive cases hides causes.
Process tracing finds mechanisms within cases; statistical methods compare across many cases.
Confounding and the counterfactual are the heart of causal inference.
Ethics approval, informed consent and a data management plan come before fieldwork.

en.title: Critical Security Studies: Securitisation, Human Security and Critique
en.short: Copenhagen School, human security, feminist and postcolonial critiques of traditional security.

sections.heading: Securitisation
sections.text: The Copenhagen School, linked to Barry Buzan, Ole Wæver and Jaap de Wilde (Security: A New Framework for Analysis, 1998), treats security as a speech act: saying 'security' does something, it does not just describe a threat. An issue is securitised when an actor persuades an audience that it is an existential threat and so justifies extraordinary measures outside normal politics. The school identifies five sectors: military, political, economic, societal and environmental. The referent object is what is claimed to be threatened, such as a state, nation or ecosystem. Desecuritisation means returning an issue to ordinary politics. A hypothetical case: Amina, a minister in a West African coastal state, calls illegal fishing an existential threat; parliament accepts emergency naval powers. The audience’s acceptance, not the threat itself, makes the move securitisation.

sections.heading: Human security
sections.text: Human security shifts the referent object from the state to people. The 1994 UNDP Human Development Report popularised it, stressing freedom from fear and freedom from want. It covers economic, food, health, environmental, personal, community and political security. Supporters say it captures violence and deprivation that state-centric security misses. Critics warn that it is broad, hard to measure and can justify intervention. It also blurs analysis and advocacy.

sections.heading: Feminist and postcolonial
sections.text: Feminist security studies ask where women are and how gender shapes war and security. They show that militarism and the public/private divide hide gendered violence and women’s insecurity from security analysis. Postcolonial security studies criticise Eurocentrism: the assumption that Western statehood and war are universal. They examine colonial legacies, racial hierarchies and how security is used to govern postcolonial states. Both reject the idea of a neutral, objective security analyst.

sections.heading: Redefining security
sections.text: These approaches criticise traditional security studies for making the state the only referent, privileging military threats, treating security as objective and ignoring gender and empire. They redefine security as a political construction with multiple referents and harms. The cost is that almost anything can become security, so analysts must ask who securitises, for whom, with what effects.

keyPoints: The Copenhagen School treats security as a speech act: an audience must accept an existential threat claim for securitisation.
Securitisation justifies extraordinary measures, while desecuritisation returns issues to normal politics.
Human security makes people, not states, the referent object, covering freedom from fear and freedom from want.
Feminist security studies show how gender and militarism shape who is protected and who is made insecure.
Postcolonial security studies expose Eurocentrism and colonial legacies in security knowledge and practice.
Critical approaches redefine security as contested and political, not a fixed objective condition.

en.title: Global Political Economy: Power, Finance and Development
en.short: Advanced debates on global finance, trade, production, hegemony, crisis and inequality.

sections.heading: The field and its disputes
sections.text: Global political economy (GPE) studies how markets and states shape each other across borders. At master’s level the question is not whether economics or politics matters, but how each explains outcomes. Realist and mercantilist accounts treat trade and finance as instruments of national power. Liberal accounts stress gains from exchange and institutions that reduce uncertainty. Marxist and structuralist accounts focus on class, dependence and the power of capital. Constructivists ask how ideas such as development or credibility make some policies seem natural. These are competing explanations, not a single synthesis.

sections.heading: Hegemony and crisis
sections.text: Hegemony means leadership plus dominance: one state or a coalition sets rules and supplies public goods, but also shapes others’ options. Hegemonic stability theorists see a hegemon as needed for open trade and stable money, and worry when it declines. Neo-Gramscian writers see hegemony as consent built through institutions and ideas, not only force. Ruggie’s embedded liberalism paired open trade with domestic welfare protection in the postwar order. Crises are explained differently too. Liberal views stress shocks, information problems and weak regulation. Structuralist views stress falling profitability, debt and the instability of credit. Financialisation, the growing weight of finance over production, and inequality are central to both debates. Global value chains, the cross-border splitting of production, make trade and investment hard to separate.

sections.heading: Domestic politics and case
sections.text: Domestic politics transmits global pressures. Coalitions, veto players (actors whose agreement is needed for change) and institutions decide whether a country opens, borrows or protects. Putnam’s two-level game captures this: leaders negotiate abroad while managing ratification at home. A small case: an oil price fall cuts Nigeria’s export revenue, worsens the balance of payments and lowers government oil receipts. The central bank may tighten policy to defend the naira, while subsidy reform raises household costs. External shock and domestic bargaining jointly produce the outcome. Governance institutions such as the IMF, World Bank and WTO set rules, but their authority depends on member states and on whether policies are seen as legitimate.

keyPoints: GPE asks how states and markets co-produce outcomes, not whether politics or economics dominates.
Realist, liberal, Marxist and constructivist accounts give competing explanations of trade, finance and development.
Hegemony is leadership plus dominance, and liberal and neo-Gramscian views disagree on how it works.
Financialisation and global value chains link finance, production and inequality.
Domestic coalitions and veto players transmit global shocks, as Putnam’s two-level game suggests.
Economic governance institutions set rules but depend on member states and legitimacy.
